en: The Miscellaneous Karmavācanās of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya (Sifen lü bu za jiemo), translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Sengkai of the Cao Wei Dynasty. Chapter One:
The Various Rules for Establishing the Precepts (Bhikṣu-karmavācanā). Section One: The Various Methods for Establishing the Precepts. First.
Regarding the text for delimiting the *sīmā* (boundary): two boundaries may not exist simultaneously.

If one wishes to establish a *śīma-kuṭi* (monastic boundary) within a larger boundary (*mahāsīmā*), one must first erect the markers for the *śīma-kuṭi*, with the inner and outer lines of its four sides being separated by one cubit (*hasta*).
When the attendant has finished chanting the interior once, he says, "This is the internal characteristic; that is the external characteristic.
He chants in this manner a second and a third time.
Among the assembly, those capable of performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) shall perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandhana*).
No one may receive a proxy consent (*chanda*), because the boundary has not yet been established.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so of this residence announces the marks of the small boundary for the four directions.

If the Saṃgha deems the time has come, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now intends to establish a *karmavastu* (precept platform) within these marks of the small boundary for the four directions.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so of this residence announces the marks of the small boundary for the four directions."
The Saṃgha now intends to establish a *karmavācanā* boundary (*sīmā*) within these marks of the small four-sided boundary here.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha establishing a *karmavācanā* boundary within these marks of the small four-sided boundary here, remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to establish a *karmavācanā* boundary (*sīmā*) within these four marks of the small boundary;
because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the text for binding the Great Precepts (Mahāśīla), one should next bind the Great Boundary (Mahā-sīmā).

First, one should mark the boundaries of the four directions of the Great Boundary; the walls surrounding the perimeter should not be too far out, as they may hinder those participating in the Poṣadha ceremony.
The proclamation is made three times.
One who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* within the assembly shall perform the formal act of delimitation;
furthermore, no one may receive a proxy vote (*chanda*), because the boundary has not yet been established.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so of this residence has proclaimed the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now establish a great boundary within these marks of the great boundary in the four directions, constituting a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so, residing at this location, proclaims the marks of the great boundary in the four directions.

The Saṃgha now intends to establish a great boundary within these marks of the four directions of this great enclosure, so that there shall be a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of a great boundary within these marks of the four directions of this great enclosure, for the sake of a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa, remain silent; those who do not consent, please speak.

The Sangha has already consented; within these marks of the great boundary in the four directions, for the purpose of a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the establishment of the great boundary is completed.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.

The Text for Establishing the *Akālacīvara-sīmā* (Boundary for Not Losing One’s Robes). Regarding the boundary for not losing one’s robes, there is no separate characteristic; it is established based upon the characteristics of the *Mahāsīmā* (Great Boundary), and is therefore referred to as "this residence.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This dwelling place is a single residence with a single recitation of the precepts.

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant its consent: let the Saṃgha now establish a boundary for the non-loss of robes, excluding the village and the area outside the village.
Thus it is announced.
Venerable Sangha, listen!
This dwelling place is a single residence with a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
The Saṃgha now establishes the *akalacīvara-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe), excluding villages and the areas outside of villages.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha establishing the *akalacīvara-sīmā* at this residence—where there is a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa—excluding villages and the areas outside of villages, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.

The Saṃgha has consented to establish a boundary for not losing one's robes within this same dwelling place and for the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa, excluding villages and the areas outside of villages.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld accordingly.
If two boundaries are adjacent, one must leave a space between them; they may not touch.
If one wishes to dissolve the boundary, one should first dissolve the *acīvarāpatti-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robes), and subsequently dissolve the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary).
One must not cross a swiftly flowing stream where it might sometimes cut off the crossing, except where there is a permanent bridge.
[The text for resolving the boundary for not losing one's robes: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
The bhikṣus residing in this dwelling place share the same residence and the same recitation of the precepts.
If the Saṃgha deems it the right time, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now dissolves the boundary for not losing one's robes.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
These bhikṣus residing at this same dwelling place and observing the same *poṣadha* recitation, now dissolve the *acīvara-apatti-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe)."

"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha's resolution to remain at the same dwelling place, to recite the Prātimokṣa together, and to dissolve the 'not losing one's robe' boundary (akathinīka-sīmā), let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."
The Sangha has already consented; having resolved the boundary for not losing one's robes at this same dwelling place and for this same recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the matter is concluded.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.
The Text for Dissolving the Great Boundary: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus residing at this dwelling place share a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let us now dissolve the great boundary."
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Sangha, please listen!
The monks residing at this dwelling place share the same residence and the same recitation of the precepts; the Sangha now dissolves the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha’s lifting of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for those dwelling in the same residence and reciting the Prātimokṣa together, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
The Sangha has consented to lift the great boundary for those dwelling in the same residence and reciting the Prātimokṣa together."
The Saṃgha consents, as they remain silent; thus this matter is upheld.
[The Text for Dissolving the *Sīmā*: Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now there are so many bhikṣus assembled. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha now dissolve the *sīmā* at this location.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
There are currently this many bhikṣus assembled; the Sangha now dissolves the boundary enclosure (sīmā) at this location."
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha's dissolution of the *sīmā* (boundary) at this location remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
The Sangha has consented and completed the dissolution of the *sīmā* at this location."
Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.

On the day of the Poṣadha or the day of the Pravāraṇā, while traveling on the road, if the assembly is not in harmony, the text for binding a small boundary at the place of sitting is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The seats for the bhikṣus are already full, extending as far as these seats of the bhikṣus.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now establish a small boundary (sīmā) within these seats.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
Within the seating area of these bhikṣus, the Sangha now establishes a small boundary (sīmā) at this very spot."
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the formal establishment of a small boundary (sīmā) around these designated seats for the bhikṣus shall remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has consented and completed the formal establishment of the small boundary around these designated seats for the bhikṣus."
Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
He then returns to dissolve this small boundary with the following text: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
Within the area marked by the sitting places of these bhikṣus..."
If the time has come for the Sangha, may the Sangha listen with patience: the Sangha now dissolves this small boundary (sīmā) at this sitting place.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen!
The boundary for the sitting area of these bhikṣus has been thus defined. The Saṃgha now dissolves this small boundary (sīmā) of the sitting area.
Those elders who consent to the dissolution of this small boundary of the sitting area by the Saṃgha as defined for these bhikṣus should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented; the small boundary for the sitting places of these bhikṣus has been dissolved.
Because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
2. The Method for Receiving the Precepts. Part Two: The Method for Ordaining a Śrāmaṇera. If one wishes to have one's hair shaved within a saṃghārāma, one should inform the entire Saṃgha.
If the community is not in concord, one should inform each individual dwelling of the matter before shaving the hair.
If the community is in concord, a formal announcement (*jñapti*) must be made.
Once the announcement has been made, one may then shave the hair.
One should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Sangha, please listen!
This person, [Name], wishes to seek the tonsure from [Name]."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent to shave the hair of so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
If one is to be ordained and allowed to go forth within a monastery, one must inform the entire Saṃgha.
Having made this announcement, one may grant him the going forth.
The announcement should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This person, [Name], seeks to go forth from [Preceptor’s Name].
If the time has come for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and allow [Name] to go forth.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this formal announcement, grant him the going forth.
Instruct him to put on the kāṣāya robe, baring the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, and join his palms; he should be instructed to speak these words:
"I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."
Following the Buddha into homelessness, [Name] is my preceptor; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One.
A second and a third time, it should be said in the same manner.
I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
Having completed my going forth following the Buddha, [Name] is my preceptor; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One.
The second and third times, it is also spoken thus: "One shall receive the precepts.
For as long as life lasts, one must not kill living beings.
Can you uphold this śrāmaṇera precept?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not steal.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not engage in sexual misconduct.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not speak falsely.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; are you able to uphold it?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not drink alcohol.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not wear flower garlands nor smear your body with fragrant oils.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replied, "I can. [The preceptor said:
"For as long as life lasts, you must not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor go to watch or listen to them.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, one must not sit upon high or large beds.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not eat at improper times.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not grasp or hold precious objects, whether raw or refined, used for adornment.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replies, "I am able.
These are the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera; they must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
Having now completed receiving the precepts, you should make offerings to the Triple Gem:
The Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Sangha of Bhikṣus;
they diligently cultivate the three types of action:
sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and assisting in communal affairs.
Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, [Name], request the Venerable One to be my upādhyāya; may the Venerable One act as my upādhyāya.
"By relying on the Venerable One, I have received full ordination.
The second and third times, it should be said in the same manner.
The Preceptor should say, "So be it," or "Very well."
The Sangha should place the candidate for full ordination at a location where they can see but cannot hear [the assembly]. At that time, the Preceptor should ask:
"Who among those present in this assembly is able to act as the instructor for such-and-such a person?"
If there is such a person, they should reply, "I am able.
The preceptor should then make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Preceptor, Name].
If the Sangha deems the time has come and the Sangha grants its consent, let [Name] serve as the instructor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The preceptor should go to the place where the candidate for ordination is and ask:
"Are these—the inner robe (antarvāsa), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), the outer robe (saṃghāṭī), and the alms bowl—your robes and bowl?"
He replies, "Yes. One should then say to him:
"Listen, son of good family!
Now is the time for truth and sincerity; one should speak what is true as true, and what is not true as not true.
Have you ever been a bhikṣu? If you say, "I have."
Is your observance of the precepts pure?
Have you returned the precepts according to the Dharma?
Have you not violated a nun of pure conduct?
"Have you not received the precepts with a malicious mind?
Have you not violated the inner or outer paths?
Are you not a eunuch?"
Have you not killed your father, killed your mother, killed an Arhat, or caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Are you not a non-human being? Are you not an animal?
Are you not of two sexual organs?
What is your name? And what is the name of your preceptor?
"Are you twenty years of age?
Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents given their permission?"
Are you not in debt?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not a government official?
Are you a man? A man may have such diseases as leprosy, abscesses, white leprosy, consumption, or insanity.
"Do you have such an illness?
If he answers, "No," one should say to him:
"Just as I have now questioned you, so shall the Saṃgha question you.
Just as you have answered me, so shall you answer before the Saṃgha.

Having thus questioned him, the instructor returns to the midst of the Saṃgha with his usual deportment, stands within arm's reach [of the candidate], and should make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from such-and-such a person.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, having already questioned him, please permit me to bring him forward.
The announcement is thus made.
The preceptor should call to the candidate for ordination, saying, "Come.

Once he has come, [the preceptor] should take hold of his robes and bowl, instruct him to prostrate at the feet of the Sangha, and then have him kneel with his right knee on the ground before the ordination master (śīlācārya) with palms joined.
The instructor should instruct [the candidate] to request the precepts, making the request as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, so-and-so, seek to receive full ordination from so-and-so."
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the full ordination, with [Name] as my preceptor.
May the Saṃgha grant me deliverance out of compassion.
The second and third times, it is said in the same manner.
At that time, the Preceptor for the Precepts should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from so-and-so."
This person, [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination, with [Name] as preceptor.
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that I inquire regarding the internal rules.
It is so stated.
Listen, son of good family!
Now is the time for truth, the time for honest speech; whatever you are questioned about, you should answer in accordance with the facts.
Have you ever been a bhikṣu?
If you say "I have," were you pure in maintaining the precepts?
Have you returned the precepts according to the Dharma?
Have you not violated the pure conduct of a bhikṣuṇī?
Have you not received the precepts with a thieving mind?
Are you not one who has violated the precepts of either the inner or outer paths? Are you not a eunuch?
Have you not killed your father, killed your mother, killed an Arhat, or caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Are you not a non-human? Are you not an animal?
Are you not a hermaphrodite?
"What is your name?
What is the name of your preceptor?
Have you reached twenty years of age?"
Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents given you permission?
Are you free from debt?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not a government official? Are you a man?
"A man may have such diseases as leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, consumption,
or insanity. Do you have any such disease?"
If it is said, "There is none," one should perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Preceptor Name].
This person, [Name], now requests the Sangha for full ordination, with [Preceptor Name] as preceptor.
He has declared himself pure, free from obstacles, twenty years of age, and fully equipped with the three robes and alms bowl.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Preceptor Name].
This person, so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination, with so-and-so as preceptor.
He declares himself pure, free from all obstructing conditions, twenty years of age, and possessed of the three robes and alms bowl.
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name] with [Name] as preceptor should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this same manner.
The Saṃgha has granted its consent; the full ordination has been conferred upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld.
Listen, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the four pārājika rules. If a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses, he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
"You must all refrain from committing sexual misconduct and engaging in impure acts.
If a bhikṣu commits sexual misconduct and engages in impure acts, even with an animal,
he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya."
"You must not commit this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can.
"Under no circumstances shall you steal, even so much as a blade of grass."

If a bhikṣu steals five coins or more than five coins from another person— whether taking it himself or instructing another to take it, cutting it himself or instructing another to cut it, breaking it himself or instructing another to break it, or by burning it, burying it, or altering its color—
he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya.
"You must not commit this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replies, "I can.
You must not intentionally take the life of any living being, even so small as an ant.

If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand, hands a weapon to another, instructs them to die, praises death, encourages death, gives another a non-medicinal substance, causes an abortion, or kills through incantations; whether he performs these acts himself or instructs another to do so—he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
"You must not commit this for as long as you live; can you maintain it?
He replies, "I can.
One must not speak falsely, even in jest.

If a bhikṣu, being untrue and not possessing them himself, falsely claims to have attained the state of a superior man—claiming to have attained dhyāna, liberation, concentration, or the four formless absorptions; or claiming to have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat; or claiming that devas, nāgas, or yakṣas come to provide him with offerings—he is no śramaṇa and no son of the Śākya.
"You must not do this for as long as you live; can you maintain this?
He replies, "I can.
"Listen, son of good family!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; a bhikṣu who has gone forth relies upon these as the dharma of one who has gone forth.
Relying on rag-robes is the dharma of a bhikṣu who has gone forth.
"Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
He replies, "I can.
If one obtains long-term benefits:
One may also accept robes sent by a donor, cut-and-sewn robes, or robes of the three types of dyed colors.
Relying on alms-gathering is the dharma for a bhikṣu who has left the household life.
"Within this life, for as long as you live, can you uphold [these precepts]?
He replies, "I can.
If one obtains long-term benefits:

If it is food assigned by the Sangha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day of the month, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the community of monks, or food invited by a donor, one may accept it.
"Sitting under a tree is the dharma of a monk who has gone forth.
Within this, can you maintain it for as long as life lasts?
He replies, "I can."
If one obtains long-term benefits—
such as a separate room, a pointed-roofed hut, a small room, a stone chamber, or two rooms with a single door— one may accept them.
Relying on medicinal drugs that have become decomposed is the dharma for these bhikṣu renunciants.
"Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
He replies, "I can.
If one obtains long-term benefits:
Butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar may be accepted. You have completed the reception of the precepts;

the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been accomplished according to the Dharma; you have obtained your place; the *upādhyāya* is according to the Dharma; the *ācārya* is according to the Dharma; and the Saṃgha is complete.

You should properly receive the teachings and should encourage others to cultivate merit by repairing stupas and making offerings to the Sangha; you must not disobey any instruction given by your preceptors and ācāryas that accords with the Dharma.
One should study and inquire, recite the sutras, and diligently seek skillful means, so as to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat within the Buddha-dharma.
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your efforts shall not be in vain, and the fruits of your reward shall never cease.
As for other matters you do not yet know, you should inquire of your Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
One should have the person receiving the precepts go forward first.
The text for receiving the robe and bowl is as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!
This saṃghāṭī, consisting of [number] patches and cut into pieces, I now accept and maintain, not to be separated from it overnight."
The second and third [times] are also spoken of in this way.
The remaining two robes are also accepted in the same manner:
"Venerable One, please attend with one-pointed mind!"
"This *pātra*, a vessel of proper measure, I now accept and maintain for regular use.
A second and a third time, it should be recited in the same manner.
[Then] request the refuge and reliance: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind!"
I, [Name], request the Venerable One to be my preceptor for dependence (*niśrayācārya*). May the Venerable One act as my preceptor for dependence.
By relying upon the Venerable One, I shall be able to abide.
The second and third times are also spoken in this manner.
The teacher should say:
"Do not be negligent."
If one says "Very well" or "I shall go," the disciple replies, "So be it.
3. Various Methods for Expiating Offenses. Third: The Text for Requesting the *Paryuṣaṇā-karman*. Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and concealed it.
I, Bhikṣu [Name], having committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, now request from the Saṃgha the formal act of concealment (parivāsa) for as many days as I have concealed it.
"May the Saṃgha grant me the *karmavācanā* for the period of concealment out of compassion.
[I ask] a second and a third time, likewise.
The formal text for granting the *karmavācanā* of concealment: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
A certain bhikṣu, named [Name], has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and concealed it.

That appointed person shall go to the nunnery and, having instructed the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs to gather, shall first explain to them the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed.
What are the eight?
First, even a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for a hundred years, upon seeing a newly ordained bhikṣu, should rise to greet him, prostrate before him, and provide him with a clean seat.
This rule should be respected and praised; for as long as life lasts, it must not be violated.
Second: A bhikṣuṇī must not revile or scold a bhikṣu, nor must she slander him by saying that he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his dignified conduct.
This rule should be respected and praised; for as long as life lasts, it must not be transgressed.

Third: A bhikṣuṇī should not perform an act of formal accusation (*ukkhepana*), a reminder (*sāraṇā*), or a self-accusation against a bhikṣu; she should not obstruct another’s confession of an offense, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, or the *Pravāraṇā* ceremony;
she should not reprimand a bhikṣu, whereas a bhikṣu may reprimand a bhikṣuṇī.
This Dharma should be respected and praised; for as long as one lives, it must not be transgressed.
Fourth, once a śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts, she should request the full ordination from the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
This rule should be respected and praised; for as long as one lives, it must not be transgressed.
Fifth: when a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must undergo the mānatva penance for half a month within both assemblies of the Saṃgha.
This rule should be respected and praised; for as long as life lasts, it must not be transgressed.
Sixth, a bhikṣuṇī should request instruction from the saṃgha every half-month.
This rule should be respected and praised; for as long as life lasts, it must not be transgressed.
Seventh, a bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there is no community of bhikṣus.
This rule should be respected and praised; for as long as one lives, it must not be transgressed.
Eighth: When the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed its rains retreat, they should request the three matters of *pravāraṇā* (inviting correction) from the Bhikṣu Saṃgha:
what was seen, heard, or suspected.
This Dharma should be respected and praised; for as long as life lasts, one must not transgress it.

Regarding the occurrence of the eight difficult circumstances (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) and other conditions for the abbreviated recitation of the precepts (*saṃkṣipta-prātimokṣa-sūtra*): the eight difficult circumstances are:
danger from kings, danger from bandits, danger from fire, danger from water, danger from illness, danger from humans, danger from non-humans, and danger from malicious insects.

Other circumstances include: when the assembly has gathered but there are few seats; when many members of the assembly are ill; when the assembly has gathered on the roof and the covering is incomplete; when it rains; when the *poṣadha* ceremony is frequent; when there are many matters of dispute; or when the night has already been long spent in discussing the *Abhidharma* and preaching the Dharma.
Before the appearance of dawn, one should perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
If dawn has appeared, one may not accept a formal authorization (*chanda*) or a declaration of purity (*pāriśuddhi*) from the previous night for the purpose of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*.
Depending on the distance of the location, if it is feasible to recite the *Prātimokṣa* in full, one should do so; otherwise, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If it may be spoken briefly, one should speak briefly; otherwise, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If there is an urgent matter and one does not speak briefly, one should immediately rise from one's seat and depart.
